_metadata.description: GT-WMR: Waymo-priority ground truth built from the 53 ingested papers of waymo.com/safety/research (55 total, 2 not ingested). Authored 2026-08-23 under the frozen protocol docs/eval-reports/2026-08-23-waymo-priority-benchmark-protocol.md; every excerpt machine-verified verbatim against its gold chunk at build time; absence logs recorded live during authoring.
_metadata.authoring_rules: protocol section 5; no item edited after seeing retrieval output (corrections logged below)

corrections.reason: case drift; exact DB span used

independent verifier found a quantitative SF evening/overnight split the absence_note understated; note + expected_behavior updated to disclose the near-miss (question unchanged; absence holds on strict reading)

ground_truth.question_text: In the high-resolution urban fatal crash-rate benchmarks study, how much higher was weekend-nighttime fatal crash involvement than weekday daytime, and what were the two rates in IP100MM?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: On average, weekend nighttime driving represented the highest risk period for fatal crash involvement (4.38 IP100MM) indicating 6.2-times higher risk than weekday daytime (0.71 IP100MM).
ground_truth.answer_text: Weekend nighttime driving carried 6.2-times higher fatal-crash-involvement risk than weekday daytime: 4.38 IP100MM vs 0.71 IP100MM.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: High-resolution urban fatal crash rate benchmarks for automated driving system assessment

ground_truth.question_text: Using median FCIR estimates, what share of fatal crash involvements were pedestrian crashes on freeways vs surface streets, and in what fraction of urban areas was the pedestrian type the most common surface-street fatal crash type?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: using the median FCIR estimate, pedestrian crashes were 10% of freeway and 22% of surface street fatal crash involvements. On surface streets, the pedestrian crash type was the most common fatal crash type in 46% of the urban areas.
ground_truth.answer_text: Pedestrian crashes were 10% of freeway and 22% of surface street fatal crash involvements; pedestrians were the most common surface-street fatal crash type in 46% of urban areas.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: High-resolution urban fatal crash rate benchmarks for automated driving system assessment

ground_truth.question_text: How many miles of Nexar naturalistic driving mileage did the NYC five-borough dataset consist of, and which borough contributed the least driving?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: the two years of driving mileage from Nexar in the five boroughs of New York City consisted of 139 million miles of driving. The most driving was observed in Queens County (75.7 million miles), with Richmond County the least amount of driving, only contributing 2.4 million miles
ground_truth.answer_text: 139 million miles total; Richmond County contributed the least at 2.4 million miles.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Refinements in Benchmarking for Vulnerable Road User Collisions by Comparing Naturalistic Driving and Police-Report Data

ground_truth.question_text: After initial video review of the Nexar naturalistic data, how many VRU contact events remained, and roughly what share were judged to have no injury potential?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: 592 contact events involving VRUs in NYC remained in the dataset (Table 1). Approximately 14% of verified contacts were deemed to not have injury potential
ground_truth.answer_text: 592 video-verified contact events remained; approximately 14% were deemed not to have injury potential.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Refinements in Benchmarking for Vulnerable Road User Collisions by Comparing Naturalistic Driving and Police-Report Data

ground_truth.question_text: According to the Building Scientific Consensus paper, what was the total US roadway fatality count and rate per 100M VMT in 2024, and how does the 1976 per-mile fatality rate compare to 2024?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: the current fatality burden (using the latest data from 2024) on US roadways sits at a total of 39,345 fatalities over 3.3 trillion vehicle miles traveled (VMT) [1, 2], which results in 1.20 fatalities are occurring for every 100 million VMT. This puts the US national fatality accumulation rate at approximately 108 fatalities per day in 2024. Nearly 50 years ago, in 1976, the United States had 44,525 fatalities with a societal fatality rate of 3.35 fatalities for every 100 million VMT driven. The 1976 per-mile fatality rate is nearly three times what it was in 2024.
ground_truth.answer_text: 2024: 39,345 fatalities over 3.3 trillion VMT = 1.20 fatalities per 100M VMT (~108/day). In 1976 the rate was 3.35 per 100M VMT -- nearly three times the 2024 rate.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Building Scientific Consensus on the Crash Safety Performance of Automated Driving Systems

ground_truth.question_text: Which 1938 publication introduced the Field of Safe Travel that the Field of Safe Motion model operationalizes, and what did that original field represent?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: More than 80 years ago, Gibson and Crooks (1938) introduced the Field of Safe Travel (FST), which is still one of the most influential models in traffic psychology
ground_truth.answer_text: Gibson and Crooks (1938); the FST broadly represents "the field of possible paths which the car can take unimpeded".
ground_truth.source_paper_title: The Field of Safe Motion: Operationalizing Affordances in the Field of Safe Travel Using Reachability Analysis

ground_truth.question_text: Whose conceptual framework and definition of a space-sharing conflict does the active-inference space-sharing paper adopt, and what does that definition say?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Following the conceptual framework outlined by Markkula et al.<sup>5</sup>, we adopt their definition of a spacesharing conflict as “an observable situation from which it can be reasonably inferred that two or more road users are intending to occupy the same region of space at the same time in the near future” (page 736)
ground_truth.answer_text: Markkula et al.'s framework; a space-sharing conflict is "an observable situation from which it can be reasonably inferred that two or more road users are intending to occupy the same region of space at the same time in the near future."
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Resolving space-sharing conflicts in road user interactions through uncertainty reduction: An active inference-based computational model

ground_truth.question_text: In the Collision Avoidance Testing paper, what share of serious injury risk did the NIEON reference model prevent in the responder role of reconstructed fatal-collision scenarios, per Scanlon et al. (2022)?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: the NIEON reference model was able to prevent 84% of serious injury risk in the responder role of scenarios reconstructed from real-world collisions that resulted in a fatality
ground_truth.answer_text: 84% of serious injury risk in the responder role.
ground_truth.section_path: Method to Set the Test Objective
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Collision Avoidance Testing of the Waymo Automated Driving System

ground_truth.question_text: Across the 16 reconstructed Chandler fatal conflicts, how many conflicts did the Waymo Driver prevent versus the NIEON model, and what serious-injury-risk reduction did each achieve?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: of 16 conflicts entered, 12 (75%) were prevented by the Waymo Driver, and 10 (62.5%) were prevented by the NIEON model. The NIEON Model mitigated an additional 5 collisions and did not mitigate 1 collision. In these 16 conflicts entered, 93% of serious injury risk was reduced by the Waymo Driver, whereas 84% of serious injury risk was reduced by the NIEON model.
ground_truth.answer_text: Waymo Driver prevented 12/16 (75%) with 93% serious-injury-risk reduction; NIEON prevented 10/16 (62.5%) with 84% risk reduction (mitigating 5 more, 1 unmitigated).
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Collision Avoidance Effectiveness of an Automated Driving System Using a Human Driver Behavior Reference Model in Reconstructed Fatal Collisions

ground_truth.question_text: How often are police-reported collisions estimated to occur per driving mile in the US, and what share involve an injury or a fatality?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Police-reported collisions in the United States have been estimated to occur about once per every one-half million driving miles (Blanco et al., 2016). Of those police-reported collisions, an injury occurred approximately 28% of the time and at least one fatality occurred in 0.05% of those collisions.
ground_truth.answer_text: About once per half-million driving miles; ~28% involve an injury, ~0.05% involve at least one fatality.
ground_truth.section_path: 1. Introduction > 1.1 Counterfactual Simulation in Autonomous Driving Verification
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Collision Avoidance Effectiveness of an Automated Driving System Using a Human Driver Behavior Reference Model in Reconstructed Fatal Collisions

ground_truth.question_text: How does the Assessing-a-Safety-Case paper define a 'claim', and what two properties make claims falsifiable statements?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: We define a claim as an assertion that supports the overarching safety determination and whose veracity can be confirmed and/or verified. In other words, claims are falsifiable statements (UL, 2023).
ground_truth.answer_text: A claim is an assertion supporting the overarching safety determination whose veracity can be confirmed/verified -- i.e., falsifiable statements.
ground_truth.section_path: 2. Anatomy of a Safety Case > 2.1 Claims
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Assessing a Safety Case: Bottom-up Guidance for Claims and Evidence Evaluation

ground_truth.question_text: In the Stoplights-to-On-Ramps benchmarks, what was the range of any-airbag-deployed freeway crash rates across geographic regions, and between which two cities?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: The any airbag deployed freeway crash rates varied from 0.355 (in Phoenix) to 1.033 (in Atlanta) incidents per million miles
ground_truth.answer_text: From 0.355 (Phoenix) to 1.033 (Atlanta) incidents per million miles -- a 2.9-times difference.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: From Stoplights to On-Ramps: A Comprehensive Set of Crash Rate Benchmarks for Freeway and Surface Street ADS Evaluation

ground_truth.question_text: Which freeway crash types dominate police-reported crashes in the Stoplights-to-On-Ramps data, and what combined share did the top four types reach?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Front-to-rear (45-53%) and vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) lateral crashes (20-35%) together accounted for at least two-thirds of all police-reported incidents. When combined with single-vehicle (6-12%) and secondary crashes (8-18%), these four types comprised about 90% or more of the total.
ground_truth.answer_text: Front-to-rear (45-53%) and V2V lateral (20-35%) lead; with single-vehicle (6-12%) and secondary (8-18%), the four comprise ~90%+ of the total.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: From Stoplights to On-Ramps: A Comprehensive Set of Crash Rate Benchmarks for Freeway and Surface Street ADS Evaluation

ground_truth.question_text: How does SAE J3164 define driving behaviors, per the Drivership paper?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: SAE J3164<sup>10</sup> defines driving behaviors as “goal-oriented activities enacted by a vehicle to implement a human driver’s or an engaged ADS’s (automated driving system) performance of the Dynamic Driving Task (DDT) or DDT fallback.”
ground_truth.answer_text: "Goal-oriented activities enacted by a vehicle to implement a human driver's or an engaged ADS's performance of the Dynamic Driving Task (DDT) or DDT fallback."
ground_truth.section_path: 2. What is good driving behavior? > 2.1 How has “good driving behavior” been defined, to date?
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Being good (at driving): Characterizing behavioral expectations on automated and human driven vehicles

ground_truth.question_text: What is a safety envelope model, and which three named examples does the Drivership paper give?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Safety envelope models establish a formal behavioral model which, given certain assumptions, creates a theoretical guarantee (based on mathematical arguments) that no crashes would happen if the model is universally adopted by all drivers. Examples include Responsibility-Sensitive Safety (RSS)
ground_truth.answer_text: A formal behavioral model giving a mathematical theoretical guarantee of no crashes if universally adopted; examples include RSS (Shalev-Shwartz et al.), the Safety Force Field (Nister et al.), and reachable-set models (Althoff & Dolan; Pek et al.).
ground_truth.section_path: 2. What is good driving behavior? > 2.1 How has “good driving behavior” been defined, to date?
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Being good (at driving): Characterizing behavioral expectations on automated and human driven vehicles

ground_truth.question_text: How do the standards Waymo cites define 'unreasonable risk' in the Absence-of-Unreasonable-Risk safety-case paper?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Unreasonable risk: risk judged to be unacceptable in a certain context according to valid societal moral concepts (ISO, 2018a)
ground_truth.answer_text: Risk judged to be unacceptable in a certain context according to valid societal moral concepts (ISO 26262:2018).
ground_truth.section_path: 2. A Layered Approach to Safety > 2.1 Defining Absence of Unreasonable Risk
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Building a Credible Case for Safety: Waymo’s Approach for the Determination of Absence of Unreasonable Risk

ground_truth.question_text: What share of US traffic fatalities did motorcyclists account for in 2022, what was their fatality rate per 100M VMT, and how many times higher is that than for passenger car occupants?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: In 2022, motorcyclists accounted for 15% of all traffic fatalities in the United States, with the fatality rate per 100 million vehicle miles traveled (26.16) being nearly 22 times higher than that for passenger car occupants (1.20) (NHTSA 2024a).
ground_truth.answer_text: 15% of all US traffic fatalities in 2022; rate 26.16 per 100M VMT -- nearly 22x the passenger-car-occupant rate of 1.20.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: A mechanistic approach to modeling omnidirectional motorcyclist injury risk

ground_truth.question_text: In the GIDAS motorcyclist dataset, what share of riders wore helmets, and how common was protective clothing?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Helmet usage was high (86.6%), with unknown helmet status recorded in 10.1% of cases. Notably, only 3.3% of riders were known to be unhelmeted, and helmet wearing rates were similar between male and female motorcyclists. Protective clothing was less commonly used, with 50.3% of riders not wearing any protective clothing.
ground_truth.answer_text: 86.6% helmeted (only 3.3% known unhelmeted); half of riders (50.3%) wore no protective clothing.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: A mechanistic approach to modeling omnidirectional motorcyclist injury risk

ground_truth.question_text: What were the observed front vs rear seat-belt usage rates in NHTSA's 2022 NOPUS data, and what share of killed occupants with known restraint status were unrestrained?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: The most recent data from 2022 indicates that both front and rear seat belt usage have increased over the last decade, though rear belt usage (81.7%) still lags behind the front (91.6%) [6].
ground_truth.answer_text: Front 91.6% vs rear 81.7%; and 50% of killed occupants with known restraint status were unrestrained in 2022.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Ride-hailing in the Safe System: Increased Seat Belt Compliance and Late Model Year Vehicles

ground_truth.question_text: How accurate is the automated brake-onset estimation versus manual annotation, at 0.5 s and 0.3 s thresholds?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: The result shows that the deviations between model output and manual annotations are small with 91.1% of the deviations are less than or equal to 0.5 s and 84.2% if using a 0.3 s threshold.
ground_truth.answer_text: 91.1% of deviations within 0.5 s; 84.2% within 0.3 s.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Automated Brake Onset Detection in Naturalistic Driving Data

ground_truth.question_text: In the San Francisco / Phoenix speed-compliance study, what share of human drivers were speeding, by how much did 85th-percentile speeds exceed limits, and what serious-injury and fatality reductions were estimated from fleet speed compliance?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Across the roadway-location combinations considered, 33-49% of human drivers were observed to be speeding, with 85th percentile speeds 3.6-7.2 mph over the speed limit. Serious injury and fatality reductions associated with altering the current human-driven vehicle fleet speed distribution toward one that is speed limit compliant were observed to vary by roadway from 18-30% and 27-43%, respectively.
ground_truth.answer_text: 33-49% of human drivers speeding; 85th percentile 3.6-7.2 mph over; compliant-fleet scenarios gave 18-30% serious-injury and 27-43% fatality reductions.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Potential Safety Benefits Associated with Speed Limit Compliance in San Francisco and Phoenix

ground_truth.question_text: What injury-risk level do the TARGET framework's safe impact-speed thresholds correspond to, and what does exceeding or staying under a threshold imply?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: These thresholds are associated with a 10% risk of injury at the MAIS3+ severity level. As such, serious or fatal injury cannot be ruled out in collisions with speeds below these thresholds, nor is serious or fatal injury necessarily expected in collisions which exceed these thresholds.
ground_truth.answer_text: Thresholds = 10% risk of MAIS3+ injury; below a threshold serious/fatal injury is not ruled out, above it is not necessarily expected -- they are biomechanical-tolerance collision conditions not to be exceeded.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: TARGET Setting for High Severity Collisions: Tolerance-Based Assessment of Risk for Generalized Event Thresholds

ground_truth.question_text: What pedestrian impact-speed threshold does TARGET present and how does it compare with the earlier consensus estimate?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: The threshold for collisions involving pedestrians of 34 kph (21 mph) presented in Table 6 is consistent with but slightly higher than original consensus estimates of 30 kph
ground_truth.answer_text: 34 kph (21 mph), slightly higher than the original ~30 kph consensus estimate.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: TARGET Setting for High Severity Collisions: Tolerance-Based Assessment of Risk for Generalized Event Thresholds

ground_truth.question_text: What is the key premise of active inference as used in the unified collision-avoidance model?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: The key premise of active inference is that all behavior and cognition can be understood based on the single principle of minimizing free energy.
ground_truth.answer_text: That all behavior and cognition reduce to minimizing free energy -- i.e., acting to minimize surprise over time.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Active inference as a unified model of collision avoidance behavior in human drivers

ground_truth.question_text: In the Looking-for-an-Out simulator study, how did participants' evasive steering differ across the steep, shallow, and medium incursion scenarios?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: the great majority of participants avoided collision in the steep and shallow incursion scenarios by consistently steering right (opposite direction) and left (same direction) respectively. However, in the more ambiguous medium incursion scenario, the participants' evasive strategies varied strongly
ground_truth.answer_text: Steep incursions -> consistent steering right (opposite direction); shallow -> left (same direction); medium (ambiguous) -> strongly varied strategies.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Looking for an out: Affordances, uncertainty and collision avoidance behavior of human drivers

ground_truth.question_text: How many rider-only miles did Waymo log in each of Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Austin during the 56.7-million-mile study period?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: there were 31.159 million miles in Phoenix, 18.260 million miles in San Francisco, 6.448 million miles in Los Angeles, and 0.834 million miles in Austin driven by the Waymo RO service for a total mileage of 56.700 million miles.
ground_truth.answer_text: Phoenix 31.159M, San Francisco 18.260M, Los Angeles 6.448M, Austin 0.834M -- 56.700M total.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Comparison of Waymo Rider-Only Crash Rates by Crash Type to Human Benchmarks at 56.7 Million Miles

ground_truth.question_text: For which crash types did the 56.7-million-mile study find a statistically significant reduction in Any-Injury-Reported crashes versus human benchmarks, all locations combined?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: The results show a statistically significant reduction in Any-Injury-Reported crashes in Cyclist, Motorcyclist, Pedestrian, Secondary Crash, Single Vehicle, V2V Intersection, and V2V Lateral crash types in all locations combined.
ground_truth.answer_text: Cyclist, Motorcyclist, Pedestrian, Secondary Crash, Single Vehicle, V2V Intersection, and V2V Lateral.
ground_truth.section_path: Crash Rate Comparison by Crash Type
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Comparison of Waymo Rider-Only Crash Rates by Crash Type to Human Benchmarks at 56.7 Million Miles

ground_truth.question_text: How was Waymo rider-only mileage distributed across S2-cell police-reported crash-rate quantiles relative to human driving, and why does that matter for benchmarking?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Waymo RO mileage in San Francisco and Phoenix is disproportionately concentrated in buckets with higher human crash rates.
ground_truth.answer_text: RO mileage is disproportionately concentrated in higher-crash-rate S2 cells (SF and especially SF; less pronounced in Phoenix), so a naive comparison against an unadjusted human benchmark ignores where Waymo actually drives.
ground_truth.section_path: Crash Rate Dependencies on Spatial Distributions
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Dynamic Benchmarks: Spatial and Temporal Alignment for ADS Performance Evaluation

ground_truth.question_text: Over the 25.3 million fully autonomous miles, how many third-party property-damage and bodily-injury claims did the Waymo ADS generate, and how many would the overall driving-population benchmark be expected to produce over the same exposure?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: the Waymo ADS yielded nine property damage and two bodily injury claims, arising from 10 unique collisions, over 25.3 million miles.
ground_truth.answer_text: 9 property-damage and 2 bodily-injury claims from 10 unique collisions; the overall driving-population benchmark expected 78 PD and 26 BI claims over equivalent exposure.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Do Autonomous Vehicles Outperform Latest-Generation Human-Driven Vehicles? A Comparison to Waymo's Auto Liability Insurance Claims at 25 Million Miles

ground_truth.question_text: What multiplicative reductions in third-party claim rates did the Waymo ADS show versus the status-quo on-road fleet, for property damage and bodily injury?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: This represents a 9-times reduction in property damage (3.08 to 0.36) and 12-times reduction in bodily injury (1.04 to 0.08) claims to the overall on-road vehicles in the areas that the Waymo ADS currently operates (the status quo).
ground_truth.answer_text: 9x reduction in property damage (3.08 -> 0.36) and 12x reduction in bodily injury (1.04 -> 0.08) claim rates.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Do Autonomous Vehicles Outperform Latest-Generation Human-Driven Vehicles? A Comparison to Waymo's Auto Liability Insurance Claims at 25 Million Miles

ground_truth.question_text: In the dense-urban VRU baseline study, how many video-verified collision events were reconstructed and how did they split across pedestrians, cyclists, and motorcyclists? What share occurred at intersections?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: A total of 335 collision events were video verified and reconstructed, of which 126 involved pedestrians, 144 involved cyclists, and the remaining 65 involved motorcyclists.
ground_truth.answer_text: 335 events: 126 pedestrian, 144 cyclist, 65 motorcyclist; more than 75% occurred at roadway intersections.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Baseline vulnerable road user injury risk in multiple U.S. dense urban driving environments

ground_truth.question_text: Across the 523 real-world VRU collision videos, how often did VRUs attempt an avoidance manoeuvre, and how does that change when the VRU was judged to have seen the vehicle?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: VRU avoidance manoeuvres were observed in 54% of all events (Table I). However, when only considering those events in which the VRU was deemed to observe the vehicle, the proportion of VRUs engaging in an avoidance manoeuvre of some kind increased to 89%.
ground_truth.answer_text: 54% overall, rising to 89% among events where the VRU observed the vehicle.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Characterising Vulnerable Road User Evasive Manoeuvring in Real-World Crashes: Injury Risk Implications

ground_truth.question_text: In micro-mobility swerving trials, which device came closest to pedestrians' lateral acceleration performance?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Interestingly, the only MMV with statistically comparable swerving performance to the pedestrian was the T-scooter during the initial region of the swerve maneuver
ground_truth.answer_text: The T-scooter -- the only MMV statistically comparable to pedestrians during the initial swerve region.
ground_truth.section_path: 3.Results > 3.2. Swerving Trials > 3.2.1. Experiment results and statistical analysis
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Kinematic Characterization of Micro-Mobility Vehicles During Evasive Maneuvers

ground_truth.question_text: Which two driving scenarios did the resolving-uncertainty-on-the-fly active-inference model apply itself to?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: two different driving scenarios that require the control of uncertainty: (1) passing an occluding object and (2) visually time sharing gaze between driving and a secondary task
ground_truth.answer_text: (1) Passing an occluding object (possible hidden pedestrian); (2) visual time sharing between driving and a secondary task.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Resolving uncertainty on the fly: Modeling adaptive driving behavior as active inference

ground_truth.question_text: How were the first 7.14 million rider-only miles distributed across Phoenix, San Francisco, and Los Angeles?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: this study considered the first 7.14 million miles of driving by the Waymo RO service, which drove 5.34 million miles in Phoenix, 1.76 million miles in San Francisco, and 0.0467 million (i.e., 46.7 thousand) miles in Los Angeles.
ground_truth.answer_text: Phoenix 5.34M; San Francisco 1.76M; Los Angeles 0.0467M (46.7 thousand).
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Comparison of Waymo Rider-Only Crash Data to Human Benchmarks at 7.1 Million Miles

ground_truth.question_text: Against the Flannagan et al. (2023) ride-hailing naturalistic benchmark in San Francisco, what was the human any-injury IPMM, the Waymo RO IPMM, and the ADS-to-human rate ratio?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: | Flannagan et al. (2023) Ride-hailingNDS | San Francisco | 64.9 | 8.0 | 0.12\* | 0.06 | 0.22 |
ground_truth.answer_text: Human benchmark 64.9 IPMM vs Waymo RO 8.0 IPMM -- a statistically significant rate ratio of 0.12 (95% CI 0.06-0.22).
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Comparison of Waymo Rider-Only Crash Data to Human Benchmarks at 7.1 Million Miles

ground_truth.question_text: What common error does the police-reported-benchmarks paper identify in how some publications compared human and ADS crash rates?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: We identified multiple publications that improperly compared human crash-level rates to ADS vehicle-level rates (Banerjee et al.
ground_truth.answer_text: They compared human crash-level rates against ADS vehicle-level rates -- the appropriate benchmark for an ADS vehicle-level rate is also a vehicle-level (crashed vehicles per VMT) human rate.
ground_truth.section_path: A.4. Errors When Computing a Vehicle-level Crash Rate
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Benchmarks for Retrospective Automated Driving System Crash Rate Analysis Using Police-Reported Crash Data

ground_truth.question_text: Why was helmet use excluded from the cyclist injury-risk models?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: First, helmet use in this GIDAS sample was only observed in approximately 17% of all cases. Secondly, the effect of helmet use is only relevant for head injuries and/ or instances where the cyclist’s head is impacted.
ground_truth.answer_text: Helmet use appeared in only ~17% of cases, and its effect matters only for head injuries -- the models assess generalized whole-body injury risk.
ground_truth.section_path: Excluding helmet status from risk models
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Bridging the gap: Mechanistic-based cyclist injury risk curves using two decades of crash data

ground_truth.question_text: For which impact configurations were pedestrian injury-risk functions developed in the passenger/heavy-vehicle study, and why not the others?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Due to a low number of cases with MAIS3+ level for side and rear crashes (Fig. 3.4) injury risk functions have only been developed for pedestrian frontal collisions.
ground_truth.answer_text: Frontal collisions only -- too few MAIS3+ side and rear cases to fit functions.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Passenger and heavy vehicle collisions with pedestrians: Assessment of injury mechanisms and risk

ground_truth.question_text: What was the overall collision rate in the LA dense-urban pedestrian dash-cam dataset, and across what range did vehicle impact speeds into pedestrians vary?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: The overall crash rate for this dataset was 0.63 collisions per million miles. Vehicle impact speeds into the pedestrians varied from 1.5 mph to 38 mph.
ground_truth.answer_text: 0.63 collisions per million miles; impact speeds 1.5-38 mph (more than half under 10 mph; 38 of 42 events under 20 mph).
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Representative Pedestrian Collision Injury Risk Distributions for a Dense-Urban US ODD Using Naturalistic Dash Camera Data

ground_truth.question_text: What generative model underlies the surprise measurements in Measuring Surprise in the Wild?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Our generative model is an evolution of the Multipath model (Chai et al. (2019)) using the Wayformer encoder (Nayakanti et al. (2022)), which produces probabilistic predictions about how a trafic situation will play out.
ground_truth.answer_text: An evolution of the Multipath model using the Wayformer encoder, producing probabilistic predictions of how traffic situations unfold.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Measuring Surprise in the Wild

ground_truth.question_text: In Waymo's first one million rider-only miles, how many contact events did the Waymo Driver experience, how many involved reported injuries, and how many were comparable to CISS-reported collisions?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Out of 20 contact events experienced by the Waymo Driver, the data shows that there were no reported injuries, and that only two collisions were comparable to those reported in the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Crash Investigation Sampling System (“CISS”)
ground_truth.answer_text: 20 contact events; zero reported injuries; only two collisions comparable to NHTSA CISS-reported ones.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Interpreting Safety Outcomes: Waymo’s Performance Evaluation in the Context of a Broader Determination of Safety Readiness

ground_truth.question_text: How was the AIDA driver model's reward specification motivated, and how did it compare with the rule-based IDM baseline?
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: We posit a POMDP model and formulated a bi-level optimization formulation of Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimate for the primitives of the model. To illustrate the estimation methodology we develop a model of driver behavior (AIDA) with the reward specification motivated by the active inference framework from cognitive science.
ground_truth.answer_text: Reward specification motivated by the active-inference framework from cognitive science; AIDA performed comparably to (and in certain cases better than) the rule-based IDM.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: Learning An Active Inference Model of Driver Perception and Control: Application to Vehicle Car-Following
